santa-cruz-de-tenerife.intro: Nine old trees make one walk through the centre of Santa Cruz de Tenerife, all free, roughly four kilometres on foot. The two Indian laurel figs of Plaza del Príncipe were planted in 1864 and stand 20 metres tall. One of the four Moreton Bay figs beside the Iglesia de San Francisco measures 14.27 metres round at the base. Two dragon trees stand by a fish monument and a church bell tower, Parque García Sanabria keeps a kapok ringed by four palms, and Parque de La Granja an Australian red gum and an ombú.
santa-cruz-de-tenerife.meta_description: Nine old trees on one free walk through Santa Cruz de Tenerife, from laurel figs planted in 1864 to a fig 14 metres round and two dragon trees.
santa-cruz-de-tenerife.question_meta: The oldest dated trees in Santa Cruz de Tenerife are the laurel figs of Plaza del Príncipe, planted in 1864. Most of the city's old trees carry no age.
santa-cruz-de-tenerife.question_answer: The oldest dated trees in Santa Cruz de Tenerife are the two Indian laurel figs of Plaza del Príncipe, planted in 1864 according to the municipal catalogue of singular trees, which makes them about 160 years old. The Moreton Bay figs of Plaza de San Francisco were already planted by 1914, but nobody has said how long before, so they may be as old or older. Most of the city's other old trees, its dragon trees included, have no recorded age at all.
santa-cruz-de-tenerife.question_context: Santa Cruz has one firm date among its old trees. The municipal catalogue of singular trees, presented in 2018 by the botanists Martín Osorio and Wildpret, says the laurel figs of Plaza del Príncipe were planted in 1864, seven years after the square itself was laid out. They now stand 20 metres tall. The city's register lists them without an age, so the date rests on the catalogue as the local press reported it. The same catalogue says the four Moreton Bay figs of Plaza de San Francisco were already in the ground by 1914, and one of them has the biggest girth of any tree in the city after the cardón of El Chorrillo, 14.27 metres at the base. Their real planting date could be decades earlier. Everything else is undated. Wildpret called the tamarind of Parque García Sanabria the most veteran tree in that park, but the park opened in 1926 and nobody has dated the tree itself. The dragon trees by Plaza del Chicharro and the Iglesia de la Concepción grow no annual rings, and no one has published a count of their branching. If you know any of these ages, tell us.

faq.q: Do any of these trees charge entry?
faq.a: No. All nine stand in open squares, beside a church or in public parks, Parque García Sanabria and Parque de La Granja, and none of them charges admission.

faq.q: How long does the walk take?
faq.a: The route is roughly four kilometres, about an hour of walking before you stop at anything. The four stops in the old centre lie within a few hundred metres of each other, so that part alone takes well under an hour.

faq.q: How far apart are the stops?
faq.a: Plaza del Príncipe, Plaza del Chicharro and Plaza de San Francisco are each two or three minutes apart, and the Iglesia de la Concepción is about 400 metres further. Parque García Sanabria is roughly 650 metres north of Plaza del Príncipe, and Parque de La Granja about 1.3 to 1.5 kilometres west of that park, the longest leg of the walk.

faq.q: Which is the biggest tree in Santa Cruz?
faq.a: By girth, one of the four Moreton Bay figs in Plaza de San Francisco, 14.27 metres round at the base, though the catalogue does not say which of the four. By height, the catalogue names the laurel figs of Plaza del Príncipe, at 20 metres, and the red gum of Parque de La Granja as the tallest in the urban area.

tenerife.intro: Tenerife is an island, and its old trees need a car. Nine of them stand in six towns. Two record-holding Canary pines are 150 metres apart at a free roadside viewpoint above Vilaflor de Chasna, 1,400 metres up. Icod de los Vinos has El Drago Milenario, a second dragon tree that survived a chainsaw, and a pine in the hills that the Cabildo puts at about 600 years. Puerto de la Cruz and La Orotava add a colonnade fig and a garden dragon, and Tacoronte and Arafo a dragon and a pine with a chapel round its foot.
tenerife.meta_description: Nine remarkable trees across Tenerife, from El Drago Milenario, which no one can date, to the tallest and thickest native trees in Spain.
tenerife.question_meta: Tenerife's oldest undisputed tree is Pino Gordo, 700 to 800 years, above Vilaflor. The famous Drago cannot be dated at all. Nine trees in six towns.
tenerife.question_answer: The oldest tree on Tenerife whose age nobody disputes is Pino Gordo, a Canary pine of roughly 700 to 800 years standing beside the TF-21 above Vilaflor de Chasna. The island's famous El Drago Milenario at Icod de los Vinos may well be older, but its species grows no annual rings and cannot be dated. Current science puts it at roughly 550 to 850 years, tradition at a thousand or more, and neither figure can be checked.
tenerife.question_context: Tenerife's age question has an awkward answer, because the island's most famous tree is the one nobody can date. El Drago Milenario in Icod de los Vinos is a dragon tree, and dragon trees lay down no annual rings. Current scientific work puts it near 700 years with a margin of a century or more either way; the name and the tourist literature say a thousand or more. Pino Gordo, above Vilaflor de Chasna, is the oldest tree here with an estimate nobody argues about, roughly 700 to 800 years, on a trunk 9.36 metres round, the thickest native tree in Spain. Its neighbour Pino de las Dos Pernadas, 56 metres tall, is 500 to 600 years old. The Pino de Buen Paso above Icod is put at about 600 years because written references to it go back five centuries. The island's other dragon trees are dated by counting the forks in their crowns, which gives about 225 years for the Drago de San Antonio and 200 to 230 for the Drago del Cristo in Tacoronte. The youngest is El Gran Ficus, planted in the 1870s.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Tenerife?
faq.a: Pino Gordo above Vilaflor de Chasna, a Canary pine of roughly 700 to 800 years, is the oldest of these nine with an age nobody disputes. El Drago Milenario at Icod de los Vinos may be older, but dragon trees have no annual growth rings, so estimates for it run from about 550 years to well over a thousand.

faq.q: Why can nobody agree on how old El Drago Milenario is?
faq.a: Dracaena draco does not lay down annual growth rings, so the usual way of dating a tree does not work on it. A modern study puts it at roughly 700 years give or take a century or more; local tradition and the tree's own name say a thousand or more.

faq.q: Can you see El Drago Milenario without paying?
faq.a: Partly. The tree is visible from outside Parque del Drago, the park laid out around it in 1996, but the full view of the crown and the base is from inside, and the park charges entry. The Drago de San Antonio, a few minutes uphill in a public plaza, is free.

faq.q: Do you need a car to see these trees?
faq.a: Realistically yes. The two pines stand at a signed viewpoint on the TF-21 mountain road with no direct bus, and the other trees are spread across Icod de los Vinos, Puerto de la Cruz, La Orotava, Tacoronte and Arafo, on opposite sides of the island. Seven of the nine are free to see.
